Interpretation and API contract

These outputs are exploratory. Emissions accounting, temperature conversion and the mapping from valuation spreads to physical decarbonisation remain subject to validation. Historical projections are retrospective reconstructions using current methodology and revised inputs, not archived forecasts made with information available at the time.

Backtest requests and units

trackingError=2 means 2% annualised TE; trackingError=0.02 means 0.02%. Default: 2; accepted range: greater than 0 and at most 20 percentage points. Optional trackingErrorUnit=percent makes units explicit.

Default response: {"{series, summary}"}. Summary includes target and full-period realised TE in percentage points, calibrated tilt, calibration dates and status. Series TE uses decimal units and an expanding window. Legacy array clients can request format=series.

Carbon intensity, SDG and ambition support pooled method=absolute only (the default). Decarb Gap supports absolute, sector-relative (default), sub-sector-relative and industry-relative methods. Unsupported combinations return an error rather than silently ignoring the method.

/api/cv/backtest?signal=carbon_intensity&method=absolute&trackingError=2&trackingErrorUnit=percent

/api/cv/backtest?signal=decarb_gap&method=sector_relative&trackingError=2

The former “Valuation-Aware” line is Decarb Gap; there is no separate strategy parameter. Fixed-score backtests are retrospective; quarter-lagged Decarb Gap data are not verified publication-date vintages. Calibration uses the full sample and returns exclude transaction costs.

Carbon prices and cost of equity

First request /api/cv/uploads and select the numeric ID of a completed upload. Both uploadId and method (absolute or sector_relative) are required for carbon prices.

/api/cv/carbon-price?uploadId=<completed-id>&method=sector_relative&inferenceMethod=carbon_intensity

An upload ID is a cache namespace, not an immutable dataset snapshot. Cache misses use current shared data. Reproduction requires retaining inputs, outputs and code versions; fixed random seeds are not sufficient.

costOfEquity is supported on SDG growth, decarb terciles and decarb-gap summary/timeseries: default 0.08, greater than 0 and at most 1. A common rate cancels in growth differences, so 7%, 8% and 9% change absolute growth but not differential-based rates or temperatures. Carbon prices and gap backtests use fixed 8%. Decarb bands select the highest-P/E target band and do not use cost of equity.

Illustrative category scenarios: exact shocks

Only the listed starting inputs change. The full model then evolves; other categories are not frozen. Shocks do not represent comparable effort, probabilities or category contributions.

{scenarios.map(([name, shock]) =>
{name}
{shock}
)}

Socioeconomic multipliers are not capped in the current scenario function. The standalone categories endpoint starts from 2024 indicators; the main projection's category option uses the latest nowcast. These paths are not interchangeable. Baseline alignment remains pending model remediation.

Methodology

Global Decarbonization Dashboard & Climate Scenario Analyzer

Current claim boundaries

The dashboard is read-only. Data collection, upload, reset, approvals and manual entry require the operator CLI. Re-run Analysis only invalidates and refetches client queries; it does not run a new model.

Published references are read from /api/reference-scenarios, with their own sources, release, licence and caveats. They are external references, not our forecasts or proof of model readiness.

The legacy calculation applies a CO2-only response to aggregate GHG plus a fixed 1.1°C offset. Its fixed-5-Gt milestone may extrapolate beyond 2100 and is not a 5%-of-2024 milestone. Legacy temperatures and milestones are not default outputs.

Gordon steady-state earnings-growth baselines assume fully distributed earnings and a chosen cost of equity. They are not five-year reverse-DCF growth. Peer-relative earnings-yield gaps are descriptive valuation diagnostics. Emissions intensity uses market cap, not revenue.

Temperature, carbon-price and net-zero results inferred from valuations are withheld. No defensible valuation-to-activity mapping or identified market climate expectation is established. No new scientific model is ready. Retrospective portfolio research is not validated investment evidence.
Archived legacy methodology — opt in; superseded claims, not current scientific guidance

The historical documentation below records old formulas and interpretations. Claims of climate inference, validation, net-zero, pricing and investment opportunity are unsupported and superseded by the current boundaries above. It is retained for diagnostic audit only.

Part I: Decarbonization Dashboard

Independent published scenario references

Climate Action Tracker (CAT), published 13 November 2025, is the main external reference: “Policies & action” represents current policies; “Optimistic scenario (net-zero pledges)” assumes all announced commitments are delivered. The latter is a conditional optimistic case, not an equally likely forecast. Temperatures are published median warming in 2100 above pre-industrial levels from CAT MAGICC7, not our dashboard calculation or FaIR.

These read-only references have a different inventory baseline and are not rebased, blended into headline projections, used as calibration inputs, or evidence that Package 2 is complete. Current-policy emissions low–high values are a policy-pathway range, not a probability interval; optimistic emissions are separate single values. Aggregate CO2e must not be used as native-gas input to FaIR.

IEA World Energy Outlook 2025 supports energy, electricity, transport and industry checks: CPS covers enacted policies, STEPS also considers intentions, and WEO 2025 has no updated Announced Pledges Scenario. NGFS Phase V, version 5.1 supports detailed pathways and model comparisons, but uses a March 2024 policy/pledge cut-off; its NDCs exclude long-term net-zero pledges. Neither source is an additional calculation input or a replacement for CAT’s full-commitments comparison.

CAT is a pinned release, updated only after manual source review; Re-run Analysis does not refresh it. Source and workbook links, attribution and copyright accompany the dashboard reference. Non-commercial use only; attribution and copyright notice required. Copyright © 2025 Climate Analytics and NewClimate Institute. All rights reserved.

Overview

The Global Decarbonization Dashboard provides probabilistic projections of future global warming based on current trends in technology deployment, policy implementation, corporate action, public opinion, financial flows, and observed emissions outcomes. The system employs a sector-specific forward projection model combined with Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification (10,000 simulations) to generate probability distributions for temperature outcomes by 2100. Financial flows (clean energy investment, green bonds, fossil divestment) serve as leading indicators, while observed emissions (Global Carbon Project data, atmospheric CO2, remaining carbon budget) provide ground truth validation.

Data Sources

The dashboard tracks 22 primary indicators across six categories, sourced from publicly available datasets:

Sector-Specific Model

The model divides global emissions (60.3 GtCO2e baseline from Climate TRACE) into six sectors:

Monte Carlo Simulation

Rather than providing a single deterministic forecast, the application runs 10,000 simulations, sampling uncertain parameters from normal distributions:

Temperature Conversion

Temperature outcomes are calculated using the IPCC AR6 Transient Climate Response to Cumulative Emissions (TCRE) framework: approximately 0.45°C per 1,000 GtCO2. Combined with 1.1°C of already observed warming and climate sensitivity uncertainty (likely range 2.5-4.0°C), this produces probability distributions for warming by 2100.

Regional Analysis

Regional projections show what global warming would be if the entire world followed a specific region's carbon intensity path. Each region (EU, US, China, India) has a different carbon intensity (kg CO2 per $ GDP), which is used to scale the baseline emissions in the model. This approach highlights the gap between leaders (EU) and emerging economies (India) in decarbonization progress.

Part II: Climate Scenario Analyzer

Scenario Analyzer Overview

The Climate Scenario Analyzer evaluates how financial markets price decarbonization by comparing the market valuations (P/E ratios) of companies with ambitious emission reduction targets against those with weaker targets. This reveals whether the market assigns a growth premium or discount to decarbonization ambition.

The system processes company-level data including market capitalisation, net profit, emission targets, and carbon emissions to derive four interconvertible climate measures: implied temperature rise, rate of emissions reduction, net zero year, and implied carbon price.

Conversion Chain

The four climate measures are derived from a single underlying signal — the P/E differential between ambitious and non-ambitious companies — and can be converted between each other:

P/E Differential → Implied Growth Premium → Rate of Emissions Reduction → Implied Carbon Price
Rate of Emissions Reduction → Implied Temperature
Rate of Emissions Reduction → Net Zero Year

The rate of emissions reduction (annual % decline) is the central measure from which all others are derived. Each conversion is described in detail below.

Step 1: Gordon Growth Model — P/E to Implied Decarb Rate

The Gordon Growth Model relates a company's P/E ratio to its implied long-term earnings growth rate:

g = r - (1 / PE)
where g = implied growth, r = cost of equity (default 8%), PE = price-to-earnings ratio

Companies are classified into terciles by their announced emission reduction targets (absolute or relative to sector/sub-sector/industry peers). For each date, aggregate P/E ratios are computed for the best (most ambitious) and worst (least ambitious) terciles:

g_best = r - (1 / PE_best)
g_worst = r - (1 / PE_worst)
growth premium = g_best - g_worst
implied decarb rate (%/yr) = growth premium × 100

The growth premium represents how much additional long-term growth the market attributes to companies with ambitious decarbonization targets. This differential is interpreted as the market's implied rate of decarbonization.

Negative values are meaningful: When the growth premium is negative, the market is assigning lower valuations to ambitious decarbonizers, implying that the market currently views decarbonization ambition as value-destructive. This flows through to negative implied carbon prices and higher implied temperatures.

Step 2: Implied Carbon Price

The implied annual decarbonization rate is converted to a carbon price using an evidence-based framework synthesising three independent approaches:

    {[ "Empirical semi-elasticity: ex-post evaluation of 39 countries' carbon pricing policies (Rafaty, Dolphin & Pretis 2025; Doebbeling-Hildebrandt et al. 2024)", "IAM shadow prices: IPCC AR6 integrated assessment model carbon prices consistent with 1.5-2\u00B0C pathways", "Marginal abatement cost curves (MACCs): bottom-up engineering analysis of techno-economic abatement potential at each price level (McKinsey, EDF)" ].map((item, i) => (
  • {i + 1}. {item}
    • ))}

The conversion proceeds in two stages:

Stage A: Annual rate → cumulative reduction
R_cumulative = (1 - (1 - r)^T) × 100%
where r = annual rate (decimal), T = 6 years (horizon to ~2030)
Stage B: Cumulative reduction → carbon price (lookup table)
Piecewise linear interpolation on the integrated evidence table

The lookup table maps cumulative emission reductions to carbon prices ($/tCO2). The annual decarb rate is compounded over a 6-year horizon (2024–2030) to derive the cumulative reduction, which is then mapped to a carbon price via piecewise interpolation on the table below (central estimates):

{[ ["$10", "4%", "Marginal"], ["$25", "8%", "Low"], ["$50", "16%", "Moderate"], ["$75", "23%", "Substantial"], ["$100", "29%", "Strong"], ["$150", "38%", "Very strong"], ["$200", "45%", "1.5\u00B0C-aligned"], ["$300", "55%", "Very high"], ["$500", "65%", "Near-complete fossil exit"], ].map(([price, reduction, signal]) => ( ))}
Price ($/tCO2) Central Reduction (%) Signal Strength
{price} {reduction} {signal}

For negative implied decarb rates (market penalises decarbonization), the price is extrapolated below zero using the slope of the first lookup segment ($2.50 per 1% reduction), yielding negative carbon prices. This reflects a market where decarbonization ambition is priced as a cost rather than a benefit.

Step 3: Implied Temperature Rise

The implied annual decarbonization rate is projected forward to calculate cumulative CO2 emissions from 2024 to 2100, then converted to warming using the TCRE framework:

Emission trajectory
E(y) = 60.3 × (1 - r)^y GtCO2/yr
where y = years from 2024, r = annual decarb rate (decimal)
Cumulative emissions
C = Σ max(0, E(y)) for y = 0 to 76
Temperature
T = 1.1°C + C × 0.00045 °C/GtCO2
TCRE = 0.45°C per 1,000 GtCO2 (IPCC AR6), baseline warming = 1.1°C
{[ ["0%/yr", "4,643", "3.19\u00B0C", "No action (flat emissions)"], ["2%/yr", "2,379", "2.17\u00B0C", "Moderate decline"], ["5%/yr", "1,183", "1.63\u00B0C", "Ambitious (near 2\u00B0C)"], ["7%/yr", "858", "1.49\u00B0C", "1.5\u00B0C-consistent"], ["10%/yr", "603", "1.37\u00B0C", "Aggressive decarbonization"], ["-1%/yr", "6,944", "4.22\u00B0C", "Rising emissions"], ].map(([rate, emissions, temp, pathway]) => ( ))}
Annual Decarb Rate Cumulative Emissions (Gt) Implied Warming Pathway
{rate} {emissions} {temp} {pathway}

Step 4: Net Zero Year

The net zero year is the year when cumulative emission reductions reach 95% of the baseline, derived from the annual decarbonization rate:

Net zero year = 2024 + ln(0.05) / ln(1 - r)
where r = annual decarb rate (decimal), 0.05 = 5% residual threshold
{[ ["2%/yr", "~2172"], ["3%/yr", "~2122"], ["5%/yr", "~2082"], ["7%/yr", "~2065"], ["10%/yr", "~2052"], ["15%/yr", "~2042"], ].map(([rate, year]) => ( ))}
Annual Decarb Rate Net Zero Year
{rate} {year}

For negative or zero decarb rates, net zero is undefined (emissions never decline to near zero).

Tercile Classification Methods

Companies are ranked by their announced 2050 emission reduction targets and divided into terciles (best, middle, worst). The classification can be performed four ways:

    {[ { method: "Absolute", desc: "All companies ranked globally by target ambition. The top third are 'best' and bottom third are 'worst'." }, { method: "Sector Relative", desc: "Companies ranked within their sector (e.g., Industrials, Financials). This controls for sectors where high decarbonization targets are structurally harder to achieve." }, { method: "Sub-Sector Relative", desc: "Companies ranked within their sub-sector (e.g., Ind. Goods & Services, Banks). Provides finer-grained comparison among closer peers." }, { method: "Industry Relative", desc: "Companies ranked within their industry (e.g., Ind. Transportation, Retail Banking). The most granular level, comparing companies with very similar emission profiles." }, ].map((item) => (
  • {item.method} {item.desc}
    • ))}

Annual decarbonization rates are derived from 2050 emission targets using: r = 1 - (1 - target)^(1/years), where target is the cumulative % reduction and years = 26 (2024 to 2050). Targets of 100% are capped at 99% before annualising to avoid mathematical singularity.

Part III: Decarb Gap Signal

Decarb Gap Overview

The Decarb Gap Signal identifies companies whose market valuations imply a decarbonization rate that differs from the globally projected rate. By comparing each company's market-implied decarbonization rate (derived from its P/E ratio relative to peers) against the projected global decarbonization rate (from the dashboard's historical trend analysis), the signal highlights potential mispricings in how the market values the energy transition.

A positive gap (projected rate exceeds the company's implied rate) suggests the market underestimates the pace of decarbonization for that company — a potential buy signal. A negative gap suggests the market may be overpricing transition expectations.

Per-Company Implied Decarbonization Rate

Each company's implied decarbonization rate measures how much the market values that company's transition prospects relative to its peers. The calculation proceeds in three steps:

Step 1: Implied growth from P/E
g_company = r - (1 / PE_company)
where r = cost of equity (default 8%), PE = price-to-earnings ratio
Step 2: Peer median growth
g_peer_median = median(g) across all companies in the same peer group
Peer group is determined by the selected classification method
Step 3: Implied decarb rate
implied_decarb_rate = (g_company - g_peer_median) × 100 %/yr

Companies whose P/E ratios imply growth rates above their peer group median are interpreted as having positive market-implied decarbonization rates — the market assigns them a “transition premium.” Companies below the median receive negative implied rates.

The peer group classification follows the same four methods described in the Tercile Classification section: Absolute (all companies together), Sector Relative, Sub-Sector Relative, and Industry Relative. Finer groupings control for structural differences in valuation levels across industries.

Gap Signal Construction

The gap for each company is the difference between the projected global decarbonization rate and the company's market-implied rate:

gap = projected_rate - implied_decarb_rate
Signal scoring (peer-relative rank)
1. Sort companies by gap within each peer group
2. Assign percentile rank: pctile = rank / (N - 1)
3. Convert to score: score = (pctile - 0.5) × 2
Score range: -1 (most overpriced) to +1 (most underpriced)

The scoring uses continuous rank-based percentiles rather than discrete terciles. This preserves the full ordering of companies and avoids cliff effects at tercile boundaries. The score is centred at zero (median company) and ranges symmetrically from -1 to +1.

The projected rate comes from the dashboard's historical trend analysis, which back-calculates a decarbonization rate for each year (2015–2025) based on the Monte Carlo model applied to historical indicator values. This rate evolves over time as real-world policy, technology, and investment data change.

Signal Backtest

The backtest evaluates signal performance by constructing a tilted portfolio against a market-cap-weighted benchmark, using monthly Total Return Index (RI) data to calculate returns.

Benchmark
r_bench = Σ (w_i × r_i), where w_i = MV_i / ΣMV
Market-cap-weighted return across all companies with valid RI data
Portfolio weight tilting
w_portfolio_i = w_bench_i + (score_i × tiltScale × w_bench_i)
Positive scores overweight; negative scores underweight. Weights floored at zero.
Tracking error constraint
tiltScale calibrated via binary search so that annualised TE ≈ target
TE = σ(active returns) × √12, target default = 2%

The tilt scale is calibrated using binary search (up to 20 iterations) to match the target tracking error within 2% relative tolerance on the full sample. This is ex-post calibration, not an ex-ante risk guarantee; check the returned realised TE and calibration status.

Monthly returns with absolute value exceeding 50% are excluded as outliers to prevent data quality issues from distorting results.
